title: What Triggers a Google AI Overview? (And When It Doesn't Show)
metaTitle: What Triggers a Google AI Overview?
metaDescription: Google decides per query, and questions and long searches trigger AI Overviews most. See measured rates, when none appears, and how to check your queries.
shortAnswer: Google publishes no trigger list. It says AI Overviews appear only when its systems judge them additive to classic Search, so they often don't. Measured data shows the pattern: informational, question-style and longer queries trigger them most; navigational, local, news and shopping queries rarely do. Rates also swing from month to month, so test your own queries.
intro: You cannot switch an AI Overview on for a query, and no study can tell you whether yours will show one tomorrow. What you can do is learn the pattern, check your own queries, and make sure your pages are eligible when an overview does appear. Below: Google's own wording, measured trigger rates from three studies (each dated), and a short method for finding your own triggers.

sections.heading: What triggers a Google AI Overview?
sections.body:
Google's systems decide query by query, and Google does not publish the rules. Its documentation says AI Overviews [are only shown when its systems determine they are additive to classic Search](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/ai-features), and so "often don't trigger". Its help page says they appear when generative AI [can be especially helpful](https://support.google.com/websearch/answer/14901683), for example when you want to understand information from a range of sources.

Two separate gates are easy to confuse:

- **Does this query get an overview at all?** Google's call, based on the query. Your page has no say.
- **Can your page be linked inside it?** Your call. A page must be indexed and eligible to show in Search with a snippet, and Google lists no additional technical requirements.

Behind the overview, Google may run "query fan-out": a set of related searches across subtopics. [Google's own example](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/ai-optimization-guide) turns "how to fix a lawn that's full of weeds" into searches such as "best herbicides for lawns". That is why an overview can link to a wider set of pages than the typed query alone would surface (see [query fan-out](/glossary/query-fan-out)).

sections.heading: Which queries usually get an AI Overview?
sections.body:
Informational questions, and the longer the better. In Ahrefs' analysis of [146 million desktop results from September 2025](https://ahrefs.com/blog/ai-overview-triggers/), AI Overviews appeared on 20.5% of results overall, but on 57.9% of question queries and 46.4% of queries with seven or more words.

| Query trait (Ahrefs, September 2025) | Results with an AI Overview |
|---|---|
| All keywords (baseline) | 20.5% |
| "Reason" queries | 59.8% |
| Question queries | 57.9% |
| Yes/no queries | 57.4% |
| Definition queries | 47.3% |
| Seven or more words | 46.4% |
| Comparison queries | 26.2% |
| Single-word queries | 9.5% |

An independent dataset agrees. Pew Research Center tracked [68,879 Google searches by 900 US adults](https://www.pewresearch.org/short-reads/2025/07/22/google-users-are-less-likely-to-click-on-links-when-an-ai-summary-appears-in-the-results/) in March 2025: 18% produced an AI summary, 8% of one- or two-word searches did, and 53% of searches with ten or more words did. Of searches that began with who, what, when or why, 60% did.

Our reading: the best single predictor is whether a paragraph can answer the query. If your keywords are "why", "what is" and "how does" questions, plan for an overview. Comparison queries sit only a little above the baseline.

![Flat lay of paper question mark cut-outs on a notebook, standing in for the questions that tend to trigger overviews](https://images.pexels.com/photos/5428830/pexels-photo-5428830.jpeg?auto=compress&cs=tinysrgb&w=1200)

sections.heading: When do AI Overviews not appear?
sections.body:
Mostly when the searcher wants a specific site, a nearby business, today's news or a product to buy. In the same Ahrefs data, [0.9% of navigational queries](https://ahrefs.com/blog/ai-overview-triggers/) triggered an overview, as did 7.9% of local ones and 6.3% of "very newsy" ones. By category, Shopping sat at 3.2% and Real Estate at 5.8%.

- **Navigational:** 0.9% (21.4% for informational).
- **Commercial and transactional intent:** 4.3% and 2.1%.
- **Branded queries:** 13.1%, against 24.9% for non-branded.
- **NSFW queries:** 4%.

One old rule of thumb is wrong. Many guides say Google stays away from "sensitive" topics. In Ahrefs' data, 34.3% of YMYL ("Your Money or Your Life") queries triggered an overview, and 44.1% of medical ones, against 17.2% for non-YMYL queries. If you publish health or finance content, do not assume you are exempt.

Availability also depends on [country and language](https://support.google.com/websearch/answer/14901683), so run your checks in the market you sell in.

sections.heading: How stable are these trigger rates?
sections.body:
Not stable at all. Semrush's study of [more than 10 million keywords](https://www.semrush.com/blog/semrush-ai-overviews-study/) found AI Overviews on 6.49% of queries in January 2025, 24.61% in July and 15.69% in November. Treat every percentage on this page as a dated snapshot.

Studies also disagree about intent. Ahrefs found 99.9% of overview-triggering keywords were informational in September 2025. Semrush reported the informational share of triggering queries fell from 91.3% in January to 57.1% in October 2025, as commercial and transactional queries rose. The tools classify intent differently and sample different keywords.

Our position: use these numbers to set expectations, not to forecast. Your own query list is the only dataset that matters for your decisions.

![A red question mark painted on a mirror against a white background](https://images.pexels.com/photos/6757687/pexels-photo-6757687.jpeg?auto=compress&cs=tinysrgb&w=1200)

sections.heading: How do you find which of your queries trigger one?
sections.body:
Combine Search Console with a hand check of your own queries. Search Console shows which of your pages were shown in AI features. A manual pass shows which queries produce an overview. Run both monthly, because the rates move.

1. **Open the Generative AI performance report in Search Console.** It shows [impressions of your links in AI Overviews and AI Mode](https://support.google.com/webmasters/answer/16984139) over time. Google said it rolled out to all websites worldwide as of August 31, 2026, though a site needs enough impressions to see it. Its documented dimensions are pages, countries, dates and devices, so it tells you which pages appear, not which queries trigger.
2. **Hand-check 20-30 queries that matter.** Search each in the country you sell in. Record whether an overview appears and whether you are linked. This is slow but it is the only way to get queries.
3. **Use a rank tracker's SERP-feature filter.** Ahrefs says its [Keywords Explorer lets you filter](https://ahrefs.com/blog/ai-overview-triggers/) for keywords that trigger an AI Overview.
4. **Check whether AI engines name you at all.** AEOeye's free audit asks ChatGPT three buyer questions; the $29 full report adds Google AI, Claude, Gemini and Perplexity. [Run the free audit](/) to see where you stand first.

sections.heading: Can you opt out of AI Overviews?
sections.body:
Yes, since Google rolled out the Search generative AI control to all websites worldwide as of August 31, 2026. It lives in Search Console under Settings, and it is a site-wide choice. Older advice that "you can't opt out" is out of date.

The [control's documentation](https://support.google.com/webmasters/answer/16908024) says what excluding your site means:

- Your links and content stop appearing in AI Overviews, AI Mode and generative features in Discover, and stop being used to ground their answers.
- You get no impressions or traffic from those features.
- It is not a ranking or inclusion signal for other parts of Search.
- It does not limit AI training; that is what Google-Extended is for.
- It generally takes a few days to take effect.

Our view: most brands should not opt out. Excluding yourself removes you from the place buyers now read the answer, and rivals' content still fills the space. The case for it is narrow: content you sell, such as paid research, where a free summary replaces the product.

sections.heading: What should you do about AI Overviews?
sections.body:
Aim to be a page an overview links to, rather than trying to make one appear. Confirm your pages are indexable with snippets allowed, answer each question once and well, and watch impressions as well as clicks.

- **Remove blockers.** Google's [AI features guide](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/ai-features) names `nosnippet`, `data-nosnippet`, `max-snippet` and `noindex` as the controls that limit what shows in Search. Use them on purpose, not by accident.
- **One strong page per question.** Google's [optimization guide](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/ai-optimization-guide) warns that creating separate pages for every fan-out variation, primarily to manipulate AI responses, violates its scaled content abuse policy. We acted on the same lesson: on 2026-10-03 we merged 165 of our own pages into 42.
- **Expect fewer clicks on triggering queries.** In Pew's data, visits with an AI summary led to a traditional result click [8% of the time, against 15%](https://www.pewresearch.org/short-reads/2025/07/22/google-users-are-less-likely-to-click-on-links-when-an-ai-summary-appears-in-the-results/) without one. Our [AI Overviews and your traffic](/blog/ai-overviews-and-your-traffic) analysis covers measuring that.

For the step-by-step playbook, read [how to rank in AI Overviews](/guides/how-to-rank-in-ai-overviews). For background on the feature, see [what is an AI Overview](/blog/what-is-an-ai-overview).

keyTakeaways: Google publishes no trigger list; it says overviews appear only when its systems judge them additive to classic Search.
Questions and long queries trigger them most (57.9% of questions and 46.4% of 7+ word queries in Ahrefs' September 2025 data); navigational and local queries rarely do (0.9% and 7.9%).
Sensitive topics are not exempt: 34.3% of YMYL queries and 44.1% of medical ones triggered an overview.
Rates swing by month (Semrush: 6.49% in January 2025, 24.61% in July, 15.69% in November), so check your own queries regularly.
Sites can opt out in Search Console, but most brands should not: exclusion removes your links from AI Overviews and AI Mode entirely.

faqs.q: Do AI Overviews show for every search?
faqs.a: No. Google says they appear only when its systems judge them additive to classic Search, so they often don't trigger. Ahrefs measured them on 20.5% of 146 million desktop results in September 2025, and Pew found 18% of US searches in March 2025. Rates differ by query type and change over time.

faqs.q: Can I opt my site out of AI Overviews?
faqs.a: Yes. Search Console's Search generative AI control, rolled out to all websites as of August 31, 2026, can exclude your links and content from AI Overviews, AI Mode and Discover's generative features. It is not a ranking signal for other parts of Search, and Google-Extended is the separate control for AI training.

faqs.q: Do AI Overviews appear for branded searches?
faqs.a: Less often than for non-branded ones. Ahrefs found overviews on 13.1% of branded queries against 24.9% of non-branded in September 2025, and on just 0.9% of navigational queries. Category and comparison queries, where your brand may or may not be cited, trigger more often.

faqs.q: Why did an AI Overview disappear for my query?
faqs.a: Google decides per query whether an overview is additive, and trigger rates move over time: Semrush measured 24.61% of queries in July 2025 and 15.69% in November. A disappearance can reflect a threshold change or a change in the sources available. Re-check the query over several days before reading anything into it.
